findings.title: Root guest-agent RPC socket is chmod 0777, so any local guest user can drive the root daemon's API
findings.impact: Any unprivileged user, service account or escaped container inside the guest VM can connect to /run/lima-guestagent.sock and speak the guest-agent gRPC API as a fully trusted peer. That API is served by a process that has just asserted it is uid 0, and it carries a port-forwarding TunnelServer, so a local unprivileged caller can make the root daemon open and proxy connections on its behalf (bypassing any peer-credential or bind-address restriction that would apply to the caller's own uid) and can read the guest's live port/event state. There is no authentication anywhere on this path.
findings.evidence: daemon_linux.go:88 refuses to run unless os.Geteuid() == 0. Line 137 creates the UNIX socket, line 141 then does os.Chmod(socket, 0o777) - world read/write/execute, i.e. connectable by every uid in the guest. Line 148 hands that listener straight to server.StartServer(ctx, l, &server.GuestServer{Agent: agent, TunnelS: portfwdserver.NewTunnelServer()}) with no credentials, no peer check and no interceptor. The same file proves the intended trust model is host-only: the vsock branch (lines 27-48, 133-134) wraps its listener in cidFilteredListener to reject every peer whose CID is not hostCID, logging "rejected vsock connection from unauthorized CID". The identical service is therefore locked to the host on one transport and opened to every local uid on another.
findings.recommendation: Do not widen the socket to 0777. Restrict it to the single principal that needs it (the lima user the host connects as): os.Chown(socket, limaUID, limaGID) plus 0o600, or 0o660 with a dedicated lima group. Set the mode before the socket is published rather than chmod-ing after Listen, by wrapping lc.Listen in a umask (or creating it in a 0700 directory), so there is no window at default permissions. Independently, enforce peer identity in the server for the UNIX transport the way the vsock transport already does - check SO_PEERCRED on accept and reject any uid that is not the expected one - so the RPC surface is not protected by file mode alone.

findings.title: vsock host-CID filter fails open when either type assertion does not hold
findings.impact: The only access control on the vsock transport silently disables itself instead of denying. If Accept ever returns a connection that is not exactly *vsock.Conn, or a RemoteAddr that is not exactly *vsock.Addr (a wrapped/instrumented conn, a future version of the vsock library, a test double, a TLS or proxy wrapper added later), every connection is accepted with no CID check at all - including connections from a local guest process over the vsock loopback CID, which is precisely what this filter exists to block. The failure is silent: no log line is emitted on the bypass path.
findings.evidence: Accept() is structured as three nested positive conditions: `if vsockConn, ok := conn.(*vsock.Conn); ok { if addr, ok := vsockConn.RemoteAddr().(*vsock.Addr); ok { if addr.ContextID != hostCID { reject } } }` and then falls through to `return conn, nil` at line 46. Rejection is only reachable when both assertions succeed; every assertion failure lands on the unconditional return. A security filter must be written as deny-by-default - the current shape is allow-by-default with an opt-in deny.
findings.recommendation: Invert the control so anything unverifiable is refused. Assert the concrete types and, on failure, close the connection, log it and continue the accept loop exactly as the unauthorized-CID branch does - e.g. build `authorized := false`, set it true only inside the innermost branch when addr.ContextID == hostCID, and close/continue whenever it is false. Add a unit test that feeds Accept a net.Conn that is not a *vsock.Conn and asserts it is rejected.

findings.title: lima.env is converted to an OpenRC conf.d file by a sed transform that does not escape shell metacharacters, giving root command execution when the file is sourced
findings.impact: Any value in lima.env that contains a double quote followed by $(...) or backticks becomes executable shell in /etc/conf.d/lima-guestagent, which OpenRC sources as root on every start, stop and status of the service. Values that reach lima.env include host-side configuration such as mount locations, the instance name and the user name, so an ordinary host directory whose name contains a quote and a substitution turns into root command execution inside the guest at boot, and on every service restart thereafter. Values containing only a bare quote or backslash are silently corrupted rather than executed, which is a data-integrity bug on the same line.
findings.evidence: print_config() is `sed -E 's/^([^=]+)=(.*)/\1="\2"/' "${LIMA_CIDATA_MNT}/lima.env"` - it wraps every value in double quotes but escapes nothing inside them. Double quotes in POSIX shell do not suppress $, ` or \. Verified locally: the input line `LIMA_CIDATA_MOUNTS_0_MOUNTPOINT=/tmp/x"$(id -u)"y` is emitted as `LIMA_CIDATA_MOUNTS_0_MOUNTPOINT="/tmp/x"$(id -u)"y"`, and sourcing that file executes `id -u` and yields `/tmp/x501y`. The in-file comment shows only the `=` case was considered ("Split the variable and value at the first '=' to handle cases where the value contains additional '=' characters"). The exposure is compounded downstream: the generated init script builds `command_args="daemon --debug=${LIMA_CIDATA_DEBUG} --vsock-port \"${LIMA_CIDATA_VSOCK_PORT}\" ..."` (line 54), whose escaped quotes only work because OpenRC evals that string, so these values are expanded a second time in an eval context. A value containing a newline breaks the file structure entirely.
findings.recommendation: Stop hand-rolling quoting with sed. Emit single-quoted values with embedded single quotes escaped (`s/'/'\\''/g` on the value, wrap in `'...'`), which is safe against $, backtick and backslash; or generate the conf.d file from Go where the same quoting helper used elsewhere can be reused and tested; or have the init script source lima.env through a parser that does not evaluate. Also reject or escape values containing newlines instead of writing a malformed file.

findings.title: --virtio-port is interpolated unvalidated into the root systemd unit's ExecStart and into a filesystem path
findings.impact: The virtio-port string is written verbatim into /etc/systemd/system/lima-guestagent.service, a unit that runs as root. A value containing a newline injects arbitrary systemd directives into that unit - an added ExecStartPre=/bin/sh -c ... line would execute as root on every boot. The same unvalidated string is concatenated into a device path in the daemon, so a value with ../ makes the agent open a file outside /dev/virtio-ports. The value is host-side configuration rather than remote input, so this is a hardening/defence-in-depth gap rather than a crossed trust boundary, but it turns a config typo or a hostile lima template into a persistent root unit modification.
findings.evidence: install_systemd_linux.go:121 does `args = append(args, fmt.Sprintf("--virtio-port %s", virtioPort))`, the joined string becomes the template variable "Args" (line 129), and textutil.ExecuteTemplate renders a text/template - no escaping, no validation, and nothing rejects newlines. The result is written to /etc/systemd/system/lima-guestagent.service at line 73 and activated by systemctl daemon-reload/enable/start at lines 86-102. The "Binary" value from os.Executable() (line 111, 128) is interpolated with the same absence of escaping, so a path containing a space or a systemd '%' specifier also corrupts ExecStart. The same string reaches daemon_linux.go:122 as `serialport.Listen("/dev/virtio-ports/" + virtioPort)`, a raw path concatenation with no filepath.Clean or containment check.
findings.recommendation: Validate virtio-port at flag-parse time in both subcommands against a strict allow-list such as ^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*$ and return an error otherwise; that single check closes both the unit-injection and the path-traversal shape. Additionally, reject any rendered unit containing a newline inside the ExecStart value, and quote Binary and Args per systemd's escaping rules rather than pasting them in raw.

findings.title: Guest-agent integrity check treats "both reads failed" as "binary is up to date"
findings.impact: If the cidata image is missing or unreadable at boot, the comparison that decides whether to install the guest agent silently succeeds and the script reports the binary as up to date without installing anything. On OpenRC guests this then reaches `exit 0` and the boot is reported as fully successful with a missing or stale guest agent, rather than failing loudly. The check that is supposed to guarantee the running agent matches the one the host shipped is therefore not a guarantee: it passes when nothing could be verified at all.
findings.evidence: `if [ "$(sha256sum <"${LIMA_CIDATA_MNT}"/lima-guestagent)" = "$(sha256sum <"${LIMA_CIDATA_GUEST_INSTALL_PREFIX}"/bin/lima-guestagent 2>/dev/null)" ]`. Both operands are command substitutions inside an `if` condition, where `set -e` is suppressed, so a failed redirect yields the empty string instead of aborting. Two failed reads both produce "", and "" = "" is true, so the else-branch `install -m 755` never runs and guestagent_updated stays false. Verified locally: comparing sha256sum of two nonexistent paths reports EQUAL. With guestagent_updated=false, lines 59-64 then match the previously written conf.d/init.d hashes and `exit 0`. A related failure on the same pattern: line 66 `print_config >/etc/conf.d/lima-guestagent` truncates the file before sed runs, so a transient read failure of lima.env leaves an empty root config behind.
findings.recommendation: Capture the two hashes into separate variables with explicit error handling, fail hard if the source file cannot be read (`[ -r "${LIMA_CIDATA_MNT}/lima-guestagent" ] || exit 1`), and test the destination with `[ -e ... ]` instead of hiding its absence behind `2>/dev/null`. Never let an empty-vs-empty comparison stand in for a successful match. For line 66, render to a temporary file and mv it into place so a failed generation cannot truncate the live config.

findings.title: Boot script chowns mount points as root without checking they are real directories rather than symlinks
findings.impact: chown dereferences symlinks. If any mount point path, or a directory component of it, is a symlink under the control of a non-root guest user when the boot script runs, root hands ownership of the symlink's target to the lima user's uid. Because lima re-runs these boot scripts on every VM start, an attacker who gains any unprivileged foothold in the guest can plant the link and wait for the next reboot to have a directory of their choosing re-owned. Reachability is conditional - it requires a mount point located somewhere the attacker can write - which is why this is rated low rather than higher.
findings.evidence: Lines 14-16 run `mkdir -p "${mountpoint}"` then `chown "${LIMA_CIDATA_UID}:${gid}" "${mountpoint}"` with no check of what ${mountpoint} actually is. mkdir -p succeeds silently when the path is a symlink pointing at an existing directory, and chown without --no-dereference then follows it. The whole loop runs as root (the systemd branch below uses sudo only because the script may be invoked non-root; the mkdir/install calls at lines 21-26 assume root).
findings.recommendation: Verify the target before changing ownership: after mkdir -p, require `[ -d "${mountpoint}" ] && [ ! -L "${mountpoint}" ]` and abort otherwise, or create and own the directory in one non-following operation with `install -d -o "${LIMA_CIDATA_UID}" -g "${gid}" -m 0755 "${mountpoint}"`. Resolving the path with realpath and asserting it is still the expected location before chown would also close the intermediate-component case.

findings.title: eval-based indirect expansion glob-expands and whitespace-collapses the mount point before root creates and chowns it
findings.impact: The mount point path handed to the root mkdir/chown is not the configured path. Because `eval echo $VAR` subjects the value to word splitting and pathname expansion, a mount point containing a glob metacharacter resolves to whatever file already matches that pattern on disk, and one containing consecutive whitespace is silently collapsed. The guaranteed consequence is that the wrong directory is created and chowned; the security consequence is that a local unprivileged user who can create a path matching the pattern can steer root's chown onto a target of their choosing, without needing the symlink of F-006. For the record, this eval is not a command-injection vector - I tested it and $(...) inside the value is not re-evaluated - but the expansion side effects are real.
findings.evidence: Lines 12-13: `mountpointvar="LIMA_CIDATA_MOUNTS_${f}_MOUNTPOINT"; mountpoint="$(eval echo \$"$mountpointvar")"`. Verified under bash: with the directory `shared[1]` as the mount point and an unrelated file `shared1` present, the eval form returns `shared1` while the correct indirection `${!mountpointvar}` returns `shared[1]`; a value of `/tmp/lima/two  spaces` comes back as `/tmp/lima/two spaces`. The result feeds directly into mkdir -p and chown on lines 14-16. The eval is also unnecessary: the shebang is #!/bin/bash (line 1), so bash indirect expansion is available - the busybox-sh caveat in the comment on line 10 applies to the C-style for loop, not to ${!var}.
findings.recommendation: Replace the eval with bash indirect expansion: `mountpoint="${!mountpointvar}"`. That performs no word splitting, no globbing and no re-parsing. If the script must remain POSIX-sh compatible, use `eval "mountpoint=\$$mountpointvar"` (assignment context, which is not subject to splitting or globbing) rather than `eval echo`.
